name: Low maximum drawdown: the 8 large caps with the shallowest worst peak-to-trough fall over the past year, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. Over closes c[e-251..e] walk forward keeping the running peak; dd_k=(peak_k-c_k)/peak_k; MDD_s=max dd_k. Long the 8 smallest MDD_s, 1/8 each (ties by name). Fewer than 8 eligible -> {}.
rationale: Drawdown-based risk is what investors actually feel, and low-drawdown names may be mispriced because volatility-based low-risk screens miss path dependence; this has not been tested in the registry (r30-ulcer is a single-asset signal). Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Magdon-Ismail & Atiya 2004, 'Maximum drawdown', Risk 17(10); Lempérière et al. 2014 on drawdown-based risk; trader practice of screening for shallow drawdowns

name: Calmar ranking: the 8 large caps with the best one-year return per unit of maximum drawdown, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. R_s=c[e]/c[e-251]-1; MDD_s as in the running-peak walk over c[e-251..e] (floor MDD at 0.02). Only names with R_s > 0 are eligible for the ranking. score=R_s/max(MDD_s,0.02). Long the 8 highest scores, 1/8 each (ties by name); fewer than 8 positive-R names -> {}.
rationale: Calmar is the standard managed-futures risk-adjusted rank; it penalises the same path risk that hurts holders of raw winners and differs from risk-adjusted momentum that divides by volatility. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Young 1991, 'Calmar ratio: a smoother tool', Futures Magazine; widely used CTA ranking metric

name: Correction-state resilience: equal-weight all 40 until the average name is 7% off its 63-day high, then hold only the 8 shallowest drawdowns
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 64. dd_s=c[e]/max(c[e-62..e])-1 (<= 0). D=mean of dd_s over eligible names. If D > -0.07 return equal weight 1/n over all n eligible names (n >= 20 else {}). If D <= -0.07 hold the 8 names with the highest dd_s (shallowest drawdown), 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: Relative-strength leaders in a correction tend to lead the rebound (O'Neil's rule), and outside corrections the rule equals the benchmark, so any difference to equal weight is purely the correction-state tilt. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: O'Neil 1988, How to Make Money in Stocks (market-correction leadership); Moskowitz & Grinblatt 1999 on persistence of relative strength

name: Volatility compression: the 10 large caps whose 1-month volatility is lowest relative to their 1-year volatility, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. sd21=sample std of ret over k=e-20..e; sd252=sample std over k=e-251..e (n-1 divisor); ratio=sd21/sd252 (skip if sd252 not > 0). Long the 10 lowest ratios, 1/10 each (ties by name).
rationale: Stocks whose recent volatility has fallen well below their own norm are in a calm, accumulating regime and carry less near-term risk premium demanded; this tests the change in volatility, not its level (level is covered by the low-vol tests already ledgered). Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang 2006, JF 61(1) (volatility changes priced); Moreira & Muir 2017, JF 72(4) (volatility-managed portfolios)

name: Cross-sectional IBS reversal: the 8 large caps that closed nearest their lows on average over the past 5 sessions, weekly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 6 and every bar in e-4..e has high > low. ibs_k=(close_k-low_k)/(high_k-low_k). score=mean of ibs_k over k=e-4..e. Long the 8 lowest scores, 1/8 each (ties by name); fewer than 8 eligible -> {}.
rationale: Closing near the low repeatedly signals short-lived selling pressure that large caps usually retrace; IBS is a widely used retail reversion tool but the registry only has it on single assets and ETFs, never ranked across stocks. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Connors & Alvarez, Short Term Trading Strategies That Work (2009); QuantifiedStrategies IBS write-ups

name: Chaikin money flow leaders: the 8 large caps with the highest 63-day close-location-weighted volume flow, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 64 and every bar in the window has high > low and volume >= 0. clv_k=((close_k-low_k)-(high_k-close_k))/(high_k-low_k). CMF_s=sum(clv_k*volume_k)/sum(volume_k) over k=e-62..e (skip if sum volume is 0). Long the 8 highest CMF_s, 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: Closing in the upper part of the day's range on heavy volume is the textbook accumulation footprint; the registry has CMF only as a single-asset signal, not as a cross-sectional rank. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Chaikin (1980s) money flow; Murphy, Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (1999); Granville OBV/accumulation tradition

name: Shadow pressure: the 8 large caps with the most lower-shadow minus upper-shadow over the past month, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 21 and high > low on every bar of k=e-20..e. For bar k: lower=(min(open,close)-low)/(high-low), upper=(high-max(open,close))/(high-low); w_k=lower-upper. score=mean of w_k over the window. Long the 8 highest, 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: Long lower shadows mean sellers pushed price down and buyers absorbed it; repeated absorption excluding the candle body is a different footprint from close-location measures. Source for the aggregation is this campaign's own design. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Nison, Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques (1991) (hammer / shadow logic); aggregation as a cross-sectional rank is untested here

name: Efficiency ratio leaders: the 8 large caps with the smoothest uphill price path over 126 days, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 127 and c[e] > c[e-126]. ER_s=(c[e]-c[e-126])/sum over k=e-125..e of |c[k]-c[k-1]|. Long the 8 highest ER_s, 1/8 each (ties by name); fewer than 8 eligible -> use N=min(8,count), 1/8 each, count < 3 -> {}.
rationale: A trend that covers its distance with little back-and-forth is cheaper to hold and less likely to be a lottery outcome than the same return earned in jumps; Kaufman's ratio measures exactly that and is not used anywhere in the registry as a stock rank. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Kaufman, Smarter Trading (1995) and Trading Systems and Methods (efficiency ratio); Da, Gurun & Warachka 2014 (continuity of returns)

name: Time above the 50-day average: the 8 large caps that have spent the most of the past 126 days above their 50-day mean, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 176. For k=e-125..e: above_k = 1 if close_k > mean(close[k-49..k]) else 0. score=sum above_k (0..126). Long the 8 highest scores, ties broken by larger 126-day return c[e]/c[e-126]-1 then name; 1/8 each.
rationale: Persistence of trend, not its size, is what many discretionary traders screen for ('stage 2' style); counting days above the 50-day mean is a simple stock-level version never ranked in the registry. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Weinstein, Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets (1988); Minervini, Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard (2013) (trend-persistence screens)

name: Pullback in an uptrend: among large caps above their 200-day mean, buy the 8 with the weakest last 5 days, weekly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 201 and c[e] > mean(c[e-199..e]). score=c[e]/c[e-5]-1. Long the 8 lowest scores (largest 5-day falls), 1/8 each (ties by name). If fewer than 8 eligible hold the eligible ones at 1/8 each; fewer than 3 eligible -> {}.
rationale: Short-term weakness inside a long-term uptrend is the best-known retail dip-buy; ranking the dips across stocks and requiring the trend filter tests it against the plain short-term reversal factor already in the ledger. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Connors & Alvarez, Short Term Trading Strategies That Work (2009) (trend-filtered pullbacks); Jegadeesh 1990 (short-term reversal)

name: Inverse-volatility weights: all 40 large caps weighted by 1 over their 63-day volatility, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 64 and sd63 > 0, where sd63 is the sample std (n-1) of ret over k=e-62..e. If fewer than 30 eligible return {}. w_s=(1/sd63_s)/sum over eligible of (1/sd63). Hold all eligible names at w_s.
rationale: Naive risk parity is the most common practitioner alternative to equal and cap weighting; against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names it tests whether simply sizing by risk adds value with no stock selection at all. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen 2012, 'Leverage aversion and risk parity', FAJ 68(1); Maillard, Roncalli & Teiletche 2010 (equal risk contribution)

name: Variance-ratio reversal: among large caps whose 5-day variance ratio is below one, buy the 8 with the weakest last 5 days, weekly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 254. lr_k=ln(close_k/close_{k-1}) for k=e-251..e. VR=Var(sum of 5 consecutive lr_k, overlapping windows, sample variance) / (5*Var(lr_k)). Names with VR < 1 are mean-reverting at the weekly horizon and eligible. score=c[e]/c[e-5]-1. Long the 8 lowest scores, 1/8 each (ties by name); if fewer than 8 eligible hold the eligible at 1/8 each; fewer than 3 -> {}.
rationale: Short-term reversal should work only where the stock's own price path is mean-reverting (negative serial dependence); the variance ratio is the standard test for that, so conditioning the reversal on it is a genuine refinement rather than another parameter variant. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Lo & MacKinlay 1988, 'Stock market prices do not follow random walks', RFS 1(1); Jegadeesh 1990, JF 45(3)

name: VIX term-structure beta: the 8 large caps with the highest sensitivity to weekly changes in VIX3M over VIX, weekly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Keep history in ctx.state as in the curve-beta spec. Each weekly call: a=ctx.macro('VIX3M'), b2=ctx.macro('VIX'); if either is null/non-finite or b2<=0 skip appending the macro value (append v=null). Append {v: a/b2, close:{s: b[e].close for every symbol}} to ctx.state.hist capped at 60 entries. Over the last 53 consecutive entries form 52 pairs (dV_j=v_j-v_{j-1}, r_j=close_j/close_{j-1}-1) with finite v in both; require exactly 52 pairs. beta_s=OLS slope of r on dV. Long the 8 HIGHEST beta_s, 1/8 each (ties by name); fewer than 8 scored -> {}.
rationale: The VIX3M/VIX ratio falls in stress and rises in calm; stocks that gain when it rises lose in stress and should be paid for carrying that bad-state exposure, a different factor from raw VIX beta already ledgered. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Ang et al. 2006, JF 61(1); Johnson 2017, 'Risk premia and the VIX term structure', JFQA 52(6)

name: Earnings-reaction momentum: the 8 large caps with the best average return on their 4 highest-volume days of the past year, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. Over k=e-251..e pick the 4 bars with the highest volume (ties: later bar first). score=mean of ret(b,k) over those 4 bars. Long the 8 highest, 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: The four biggest-volume days of a year are usually the four earnings releases; a stock that has reacted well to its last four reports has persistently positive earnings news, which Chan-Jegadeesh-Lakonishok found is a source of momentum separate from price momentum. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok 1996, JF 51(5); Bernard & Thomas 1989, JAR 27 (earnings-surprise drift)

name: Leader persistence: the 8 large caps that have been in the top quarter on 12-1 momentum at the most of the last 6 month-ends, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 358 (every checkpoint needs 12-1 data). For j=0..5 let tj=e-21*j; m_j(s)=close[tj-21]/close[tj-252]-1. At each checkpoint rank all eligible names by m_j (descending); in_j=1 if the name is in the top 10. score=sum of in_j over j=0..5 (integer 0..6). Long the 8 highest scores, ties by current m_0 descending then name; 1/8 each.
rationale: A stock that stays in the top quarter month after month has had steady relative strength rather than one lucky month; persistence of rank is a cleaner signal than the point-in-time 12-1 rank and is not in the registry. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Jegadeesh & Titman 1993, JF 48(1); Grinblatt & Moskowitz 2004, JFE 71 (consistency of past returns)

name: Down-streak reversal: buy up to 5 large caps that have closed lower for at least 3 days in a row, daily
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 12. streak_s = number of consecutive bars ending at e with ret(b,k) < 0 (stop at first non-negative return, count at most 10). Eligible names have streak >= 3. Sort by streak descending, then by c[e]/c[e-streak]-1 ascending, then name. Hold the first min(5,count) names at 1/5 each; if count = 0 return {} (cash). Names drop out the first day the streak breaks.
rationale: Several consecutive down closes mark short-term exhaustion in liquid large caps; ranking by streak length is the cross-sectional form of the Connors 3-day rules, and each name exits on its first up day without any tuned exit. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Connors & Alvarez, Short Term Trading Strategies That Work (2009) (consecutive-down-day setups); Jegadeesh 1990

name: Halloween beta rotation: highest-beta 10 large caps November to April, lowest-beta 10 May to October, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. m=UTC month (1..12) of the bar at e (new Date(b[e].time*1000).getUTCMonth()+1, first symbol's view). EW market return r_m(k)=mean of ret over every eligible name that has bar k, k=e-250..e. beta_s=cov(ret_s,r_m)/var(r_m) over those 251 days. If m in {11,12,1,2,3,4} long the 10 highest beta_s else the 10 lowest, 1/10 each (ties by name).
rationale: The Halloween effect says equity returns are higher November to April; if it is a risk-premium effect it should show up as a high-beta tilt in that half and a low-beta tilt in the other, which tests the effect through stocks instead of through an index timing rule. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Bouman & Jacobsen 2002, AER 92(5); Jacobsen & Zhang 2012 (Halloween effect robustness); Savor & Wilson 2014 (beta rotation form)

name: Low overnight-gap volatility: the 10 large caps with the calmest open-versus-previous-close gaps over 6 months, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 127 and every open > 0. gap_k=open_k/close_{k-1}-1 for k=e-125..e. sdg_s=sample std (n-1) of gap_k. Long the 10 lowest sdg_s, 1/10 each (ties by name).
rationale: News and earnings arrive mostly overnight, so overnight-gap dispersion isolates event risk from ordinary intraday noise; low event risk may be rewarded differently from low total volatility, which is the ledgered anomaly. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019, JFE 134 (overnight vs intraday returns); Cliff, Cooper & Gulen 2008 (return differences between trading and non-trading hours)

name: Exclusion screen: hold the other 32 of 40 large caps after dropping the 8 weakest 12-1 momentum names, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. m_s=close[e-21]/close[e-252]-1. Let n=count of eligible; if n < 30 return {}. Drop the 8 lowest m_s (ties by name); hold the remaining n-8 names at 1/(n-8) each.
rationale: Many investors use momentum only to avoid the losers rather than to pick winners; because losers drive most of the momentum spread, dropping them from a diversified book is the practical long-only version and has a low tracking error against equal weight. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Jegadeesh & Titman 1993, JF 48(1) (loser leg); Hong, Lim & Stein 2000, JF 55(1); exclusion-screen practice

name: Breakaway-gap frequency: the 8 large caps with the most opening gaps above the prior day's high in 6 months, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 127. gapup_k=1 if open_k > high_{k-1} else 0, for k=e-125..e. score=sum gapup_k. Long the 8 highest scores, ties broken by larger 126-day return then name, 1/8 each.
rationale: A stock that keeps opening above the previous day's entire range is repeatedly repricing on good news; counting these breakaway gaps measures news frequency and direction, unlike the single-gap event rules ledgered. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Bulkowski, Encyclopedia of Chart Patterns (breakaway gaps); Chan 2003, JF 58(5) (news-driven momentum)

name: Volume-price divergence: the 8 large caps where 63-day volume flow most exceeds their price rank, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 65. obv_k = running sum over j=e-62..k of sign(close_j-close_{j-1})*volume_j (sign 0 on equal closes). A_s=obv_e / sum(volume_j over j=e-62..e) (in [-1,1]; skip if the volume sum is 0). P_s=close[e]/close[e-63]-1. Rank both across eligible names ascending (rank 1..n, ties by name). score=rank(A_s)-rank(P_s). Long the 8 highest scores (volume flow strong, price lagging), 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: Accumulation without a price move is the classic divergence traders look for before a markup; ranking the gap between volume flow and price across stocks gives it a testable, parameter-light form (the registry has OBV divergence only on single assets). Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Granville, Granville's New Key to Stock Market Profits (1963) (OBV); Murphy, Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (1999)

name: Relative win rate: the 8 large caps that beat the equal-weight basket in the most 5-day blocks of the past 26 weeks, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 131. Block j (j=0..25) ends at bar bj=e-5*(25-j) and starts at bj-5. block return of s = close[bj]/close[bj-5]-1. EW basket return in the block = mean of those over all eligible names. win_j=1 if s's block return > basket's. score=sum win_j (0..26). Long the 8 highest scores, ties broken by 130-day return desc then name; 1/8 each.
rationale: How often a stock beats the market is a different measure from how much it beats it; frequent small wins reflect steady flows rather than a few jumps and echo the 'frog in the pan' idea. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Da, Gurun & Warachka 2014, RFS 27(7); Grinblatt & Moskowitz 2004, JFE 71(3)

name: Three-factor price composite: the 10 large caps with the best equal-weight z-score of 12-1 momentum, low volatility and 1-month reversal, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. A=close[e-21]/close[e-252]-1; B=-sd63 where sd63 is the sample std (n-1) of ret over k=e-62..e; C=-(close[e]/close[e-21]-1). Across eligible names compute z-scores (subtract mean, divide by population std across names) of A, B and C (skip a factor with zero std). score=zA+zB+zC. Long the 10 highest scores, 1/10 each (ties by name); fewer than 15 eligible -> {}.
rationale: Combining the three best-documented price-only anomalies is how factor funds are built (diversified signals, partly offsetting crash risks); the ledger has each alone but not their blend in one score. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen 2013, JF 68(3) (value and momentum everywhere, composite construction); Blitz & van Vliet 2007, JPM; Jegadeesh 1990

name: Rising relative-strength rank: the 8 large caps in the top half on 126-day return whose rank improved most over the last 63 days, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 190. R_now(s)=close[e]/close[e-126]-1; R_prev(s)=close[e-63]/close[e-189]-1. rank each across all eligible names ascending (1..n; ties by name): rk_now, rk_prev. Candidates: rk_now > n/2. score=rk_now-rk_prev. Long the 8 highest scores among candidates, 1/8 each (ties by name); fewer than 8 candidates -> hold them at 1/8, fewer than 3 -> {}.
rationale: O'Neil-style screens like leaders whose relative strength is rising, not just high; the rank change captures a stock that is just starting to lead, which neither level momentum nor acceleration (tested) captures. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: O'Neil, How to Make Money in Stocks (1988) (RS line rising); Novy-Marx 2012, JFE 103(3) (intermediate momentum)

name: Long-horizon intraday reversal: the 8 large caps with the lowest cumulative open-to-close return over 12-1 months, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253 and every open > 0. score=sum over k=e-251..e-21 of ln(close_k/open_k). Long the 8 LOWEST scores, 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: Lou, Polk and Skouras find intraday returns reverse while overnight returns persist; the ledger tested the one-month intraday version and the overnight 12-1, but not the 12-1 intraday horizon where their continuation/reversal split is strongest. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019, 'A tug of war: overnight versus intraday expected returns', JFE 134(1)

name: New-high frequency: the 8 large caps with the most 20-day closing highs in the past 6 months, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 147. For k=e-125..e: hh_k=1 if close_k > max(close[k-20..k-1]) else 0. score=sum hh_k. Long the 8 highest scores, ties broken by larger 126-day return then name, 1/8 each.
rationale: Stocks that repeatedly make fresh highs are in sustained uptrends; counting breakouts over a window measures trend frequency rather than the distance from a single 52-week high, and is related to but not the same as Donchian momentum. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Donchian/Turtle channel practice (Faith, Way of the Turtle 2007); George & Hwang 2004, JF 59(5)

name: Event-day intraday follow-through: the 8 large caps whose latest volume spike closed furthest above its open, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 100. An event is a bar k in [e-44, e-3] with volume_k >= 2.5*mean(volume[k-50..k-1]). Use each name's most recent event only. score=(close_k-open_k)/open_k for that event bar; names with no event or score <= 0 are not eligible. Long the 8 highest scores, 1/8 each (ties by name); fewer than 8 eligible -> hold the eligible at 1/8, fewer than 3 -> {}.
rationale: On big-news days the part of the move that happens after the open reflects informed flow rather than the overnight gap; waiting 3 sessions avoids the immediate reaction and tests whether intraday follow-through, not the gap (ledgered), drives post-event drift. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Bernard & Thomas 1989, JAR 27; Berkman et al. 2012 (opening vs trading-hours earnings reactions); Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019

name: Effort versus result: among large caps down over 5 days, buy the 8 where volume is heavy but the daily range is small, weekly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 65, close[e]/close[e-5]-1 < 0 and all prices in the window are positive. vr=mean(volume[e-4..e])/mean(volume[e-63..e-5]); rr=mean((high-low)/close over e-4..e)/mean((high-low)/close over e-63..e-5). score=vr/rr (skip if rr not > 0). Long the 8 highest scores, 1/8 each (ties by name); fewer than 8 eligible -> hold eligible at 1/8, fewer than 3 -> {}.
rationale: Wyckoff's effort-versus-result: heavy volume with little price progress after a decline suggests supply is being absorbed; the registry has the high-volume stopping-bar as a single-stock signal but not this ratio ranked across stocks. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Wyckoff method (Hank Pruden, The Three Skills of Top Trading, 2007); Williams, Master the Markets (VSA, 1993)

name: IBD-style relative strength rating: the 8 large caps with the highest 0.4/0.2/0.2/0.2 weighted four-quarter return, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. Q1=close[e]/close[e-63]-1; Q2=close[e-63]/close[e-126]-1; Q3=close[e-126]/close[e-189]-1; Q4=close[e-189]/close[e-252]-1. score=0.4*Q1+0.2*Q2+0.2*Q3+0.2*Q4. Long the 8 highest scores, 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: Investor's Business Daily's Relative Strength Rating is among the most used momentum screens by retail traders; it overweights the latest quarter and has no skip month, so it separates the practitioner rule from the academic 12-1 that the registry tests. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: O'Neil, How to Make Money in Stocks (1988); IBD Relative Strength Rating methodology (4-quarter 40/20/20/20 weighting)

name: Momentum without event days: 12-1 return after removing each stock's 8 highest-volume days, top 8, monthly
rule: Conventions: portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx) on the 40 large caps (meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_DAILY', do not also set meta.assets), long-only; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close, so only bars up to e are used); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; every window is counted back from e and includes bar e unless stated; ties are broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; a symbol lacking the bars its score needs, or with any non-finite/non-positive price in the window, is not eligible for that call; if the rule's minimum eligible count is not met, return {} (cash that period). Eligible if L >= 253. Over k=e-251..e-21 (231 bars) remove the 8 bars with the highest volume (ties: later bar first). score=sum over the remaining bars of ln(1+ret(b,k)). Long the 8 highest scores, 1/8 each (ties by name).
rationale: Chan et al. separate price momentum from earnings-news momentum; stripping the highest-volume (news and earnings) days leaves the drift earned on quiet days, which is the part Daniel-Hirshleifer style underreaction theories predict continues. Caveat: survivorship bias: the 40 names are today's large caps picked with hindsight, so long-only tilts toward past winners are flattered and any edge must be read against the equal-weight benchmark of the same names.
source: Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok 1996, JF 51(5); Chan 2003, JF 58(5) (momentum after public news)
